items.question_text: A particle travels in the xy plane under a constant acceleration 'a' pointing along the negative y-direction. Its path is described by y = px − qx², with p and q both positive constants. Determine the particle's velocity, magnitude and direction, as it passes through the origin.

solution.approach: Match the given trajectory to the standard projectile path written in terms of time, so the coefficients of x and x² give the two velocity components.

steps.text: Since the acceleration is only along −y, the horizontal velocity stays constant and the horizontal position is uₓt.
Write the vertical position using this time, with a as the acceleration magnitude and u_y the initial vertical velocity.
Compare this with the given equation term by term.
Solve the second equation for the horizontal velocity component.
Use the first equation to get the vertical velocity component, then combine the components to get the velocity's magnitude and direction at the origin.
steps.equation: u_y = p√(a/(2q)); v = √(a/(2q)) (î + p ĵ), |v| = √(a/(2q)) × √(1 + p²) = √(a(1 + p²)/(2q)), direction tan⁻¹p above the x-axis

final_answer.value: v = √(a/(2q)) î + p√(a/(2q)) ĵ; magnitude |v| = √(a(1 + p²)/(2q)), direction tan⁻¹p above the x-axis.

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the factor ½ in the vertical position equation, which gives the horizontal component as √(a/q) instead of √(a/(2q)).

items.question_text:
A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 20 m/s from a point O at the top edge of a wedge-shaped incline. Point Q lies directly beneath O, and the sloped surface of the wedge falls away at 45° to the horizontal. The ball follows a curved path and lands on the sloped surface at point P, where the angle OPQ equals 45°.
(a) Find the flight time of the ball before it lands on the sloped surface at P.
(b) Find the straight-line distance OP that the ball covers from launch to landing on the slope.
items.figure_description: O is the launch point at the top of a right-angled wedge; Q lies directly below O. The sloped face of the wedge runs down toward the base, meeting the horizontal base at 45°. The ball's curved path from O meets the slope at P, and the angle OPQ between line OP and the horizontal line QP is 45°.

solution.approach: On a 45° incline, the vertical drop equals the horizontal distance travelled, so equate them to find the time, then find OP from the two legs.

steps.text: Write the horizontal distance and the vertical drop as functions of time for the horizontal launch, taking g = 10 m/s².
The particle lands on the incline where the drop equals the horizontal distance, because the incline makes 45° with the horizontal.
steps.why_this_step: On a 45° incline through O, every point has its vertical drop equal to its horizontal distance from O.

steps.text: Solve this equation for the time of flight (part a).
Find the horizontal distance and the vertical drop at t = 4 s.
OP is the straight-line distance from O to P, the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs x = 80 m and y = 80 m.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the range OP as the horizontal distance 80 m instead of the slanted distance along the incline, missing the factor √2.
Writing the vertical drop as g t² instead of ½ g t², which gives t = 2 s and OP = 40√2 m ≈ 56.6 m.

items.question_text:
In the diagram, take g = 10 m/s².
(a) Find how long after being launched the particle reaches the ground at point P.
(b) Find the horizontal separation between Q and P.
(c) Find the particle's velocity, magnitude and direction, when it reaches point P.
items.figure_description: The particle is launched horizontally with velocity 40 m/s from point O, at the top of a vertical tower of height 45 m. Q is the point directly below O at the base of the tower on the ground. The particle follows a curved path from O and lands at point P on the ground, to the right of Q.

solution.approach: Horizontal projectile from height 45 m; find the fall time from the height, then use it for the horizontal distance and the two velocity components at landing.

steps.text: Write the height fallen as a function of time for a horizontal launch, using g = 10 m/s².
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
Find the horizontal distance QP, since the horizontal velocity stays constant (part b).
Find the horizontal and vertical velocity components at P.
Combine the components to get the speed and direction at P: the magnitude is the hypotenuse of the 40 m/s and 30 m/s components, and the direction is the angle whose tangent is 30/40.
steps.equation: (a) t = 3 s (b) QP = 120 m (c) v = √(40² + 30²) = 50 m/s at 37° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: (a) t = 3 s, (b) QP = 120 m, (c) v = 50 m/s at 37° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Adding the horizontal and vertical speeds directly instead of combining them as vectors, giving 40 + 30 = 70 m/s instead of 50 m/s.

items.question_text: For a fixed launch speed u, two different projection angles can give the same horizontal range. Prove that adding together the maximum heights reached for these two angles gives a result that does not depend on which of the two angles was used.

solution.approach: For a given range, the two projection angles are complementary; write the maximum height for each and add them.

steps.text: Two angles giving the same range are θ and (90°−θ); write the maximum height for each.
Add the two heights and use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
steps.why_this_step: The angle θ cancels out completely, leaving only u and g, so the sum does not depend on which pair of complementary angles is used.

final_answer.value: H₁ + H₂ = u²/(2g), a constant that does not depend on θ.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two range formulas instead of the two height formulas, getting R₁+R₂ = 2u²sin2θ/g, which still depends on θ and does not show the required result.

items.question_text: A car starts from rest at the origin and accelerates at 2 m/s² along the positive x-axis. A man stands at the back of the car holding a gun. He fires a bullet at time t = 4 s, and this bullet meets a bird in flight at the later time t = 8 s. At that instant the bird's position vector is 40î + 80ĵ + 40k̂. Find the bullet's velocity of projection, given that the y-axis lies in the horizontal plane and g = 10 m/s².
items.figure_description: A small illustration shows a man standing at the back of a moving car, arms outstretched, suggesting he holds a gun while the vehicle accelerates forward; no numeric values are marked on it.

solution.approach: Find the car's position when the bullet is fired, then use the bullet's projectile motion over 4 s to match the bird's given position.

steps.text: Find the car's position at t = 4 s, when the bullet is fired, since the car starts from rest at the origin.
The bullet travels from t = 4 s to t = 8 s before reaching the bird.
The x and y directions have no acceleration, so match the bird's x and y coordinates using the launch velocity components and the starting point found above.
Solve for the horizontal launch velocity components.
The z direction has acceleration −g, so match the bird's height using the vertical launch component.
Solve for the vertical launch component.
The velocity of projection is the vector with these three components, and its magnitude follows from them. This is the velocity relative to the ground.
The gun is mounted on the car, which is still accelerating, so the velocity of projection relative to the gun is the ground-frame velocity minus the car's velocity at the firing instant t = 4 s.
steps.equation: car velocity at t = 4 s = 2(4) = 8 m/s along x; v (relative to gun) = (6−8)î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ = −2î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, |v| = √(2² + 20² + 30²) = √1304 ≈ 36.1 m/s

final_answer.value: Relative to the ground: v = 6î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, magnitude 2√334 m/s ≈ 36.6 m/s. Relative to the gun (which moves with the car at 8î m/s at t = 4 s): v = −2î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, magnitude √1304 ≈ 36.1 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Measuring the bullet's motion from the origin instead of from the car's position at firing, which gives vₓ = 10 m/s and a wrong speed of 10√14 ≈ 37.4 m/s.

items.question_text: Assertion: Taking g = 10 m/s², the claim is that in projectile motion the particle's speed changes by 10 m/s during every second of flight. Reason: Acceleration is simply defined as the rate at which velocity changes.

options.label: (a)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (b)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (c)
options.text: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

options.label: (d)
options.text: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

solution.approach: Acceleration changes the velocity vector by a fixed amount each second, but speed is the length of that vector, which does not change by that same fixed amount.

steps.text: Take a projectile with both horizontal and vertical velocity components, and track its speed second by second.
The vertical component of velocity does change by exactly 10 m/s every second, since the vertical acceleration is constant.
The horizontal component never changes, and speed is the length of the full velocity vector, not only its vertical part.
Because speed combines both components through a square root, its change from one second to the next is not a fixed 10 m/s; it is largest near the ground and smallest near the top of the flight.

So the Assertion is false because it confuses the constant change in the velocity vector with the varying change in speed, while the Reason — that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — is a true, separate statement.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason describes the vector velocity correctly; the Assertion wrongly applies that fact to the scalar speed.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Confusing velocity with speed, so a constant 10 m/s change in the velocity vector is wrongly read as a constant 10 m/s change in speed.
Judging the Reason false by treating rate of change of velocity as if it only meant rate of change of speed.

items.question_text: Using the launch data marked in the diagram, work out how long the projectile stays in the air and how far it travels along the slanted surface, taking g = 10 m/s².
items.figure_description: An inclined plane rises to the right from a point on level ground at 30° to the horizontal. From that same point a projectile is launched at 20√2 m/s, its velocity making 45° with the horizontal, so that it is steeper than the incline by 15° and lands on the incline.

solution.approach: Resolve the velocity and gravity along and perpendicular to the incline; the projectile lands on the incline when the perpendicular displacement returns to zero.

steps.text: In the figure the velocity is drawn steeper than the incline. It makes 45° with the horizontal while the incline makes 30° with the horizontal, both measured from the same point at the base of the incline. So the velocity makes 45° minus 30° with the incline surface, and the projectile lands further up the slope.
steps.why_this_step: The angle between the velocity and the incline surface, not the angle with the horizontal, decides the motion along the incline.

steps.text: Take axes along the incline and perpendicular to it. Resolve the initial velocity into these two directions, and resolve gravity the same way.
steps.equation: along incline: u cos15° ; perpendicular: u sin15° ; g along incline: g sin30° ; g perpendicular: g cos30°

steps.text: The projectile returns to the incline surface when the perpendicular displacement becomes zero again. This gives the time of flight.
Range along the incline is the along-incline distance covered in time T, using the along-incline part of gravity that slows the climb.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the incline and using the flat-ground formulas T = 2u sinθ/g and R = u² sin2θ/g gives T = 4 s and R = 80 m, missing that the ground here is sloped.
Using the angle sum 45°+30° instead of the difference 45°−30° gives T ≈ 6.31 s and R ≈ 145.71 m, which is the answer for the projectile fired down the incline, not up it.
